source: “In vain it was to rake for Ambergriese in the paunch of this Leviathan, insufferable fetor denying not inquiry.” Sir T. Browne, V.E.

It was a week or two after the last whaling scene recounted, and when we were slowly sailing over a sleepy, vapory, mid-day sea, that the many noses on the Pequod’s deck proved more vigilant discoverers than the three pairs of eyes aloft. A peculiar and not very pleasant smell was smelt in the sea.
“I will bet something now,” said Stubb, “that somewhere hereabouts are some of those drugged whales we tickled the other day. I thought they would keel up before long.”

Presently, the vapors in advance slid aside; and there in the distance lay a ship, whose furled sails betokened that some sort of whale must be alongside. As we glided nearer, the stranger showed French colours from his peak; and by the eddying cloud of vulture sea-fowl that circled, and hovered, and swooped around him, it was plain that the whale alongside must be what the fishermen call a blasted whale, that is, a whale that has died unmolested on the sea, and so floated an unappropriated corpse. It may well be conceived, what an unsavory odor such a mass must exhale; worse than an Assyrian city in the plague, when the living are incompetent to bury the departed. So intolerable indeed is it regarded by some, that no cupidity could persuade them to moor alongside of it. Yet are there those who will still do it; notwithstanding the fact that the oil obtained from such subjects is of a very inferior quality, and by no means of the nature of attar-of-rose.

Coming still nearer with the expiring breeze, we saw that the Frenchman had a second whale alongside; and this second whale seemed even more of a nosegay than the first. In truth, it turned out to be one of those problematical whales that seem to dry up and die with a sort of prodigious dyspepsia, or indigestion; leaving their defunct bodies almost entirely bankrupt of anything like oil. Nevertheless, in the proper place we shall see that no knowing fisherman will ever turn up his nose at such a whale as this, however much he may shun blasted whales in general.
The Pequod had now swept so nigh to the stranger, that Stubb vowed he recognised his cutting spade-pole entangled in the lines that were knotted round the tail of one of these whales.

“There’s a pretty fellow, now,” he banteringly laughed, standing in the ship’s bows, “there’s a jackal for ye! I well know that these Crappoes of Frenchmen are but poor devils in the fishery; sometimes lowering their boats for breakers, mistaking them for Sperm Whale spouts; yes, and sometimes sailing from their port with their hold full of boxes of tallow candles, and cases of snuffers, foreseeing that all the oil they will get won’t be enough to dip the Captain’s wick into; aye, we all know these things; but look ye, here’s a Crappo that is content with our leavings, the drugged whale there, I mean; aye, and is content too with scraping the dry bones of that other precious fish he has there. Poor devil! I say, pass round a hat, some one, and let’s make him a present of a little oil for dear charity’s sake. For what oil he’ll get from that drugged whale there, wouldn’t be fit to burn in a jail; no, not in a condemned cell. And as for the other whale, why, I’ll agree to get more oil by chopping up and trying out these three masts of ours, than he’ll get from that bundle of bones; though, now that I think of it, it may contain something worth a good deal more than oil; yes, ambergris. I wonder now if our old man has thought of that. It’s worth trying. Yes, I’m for it;” and so saying he started for the quarter-deck.

By this time the faint air had become a complete calm; so that whether or no, the Pequod was now fairly entrapped in the smell, with no hope of escaping except by its breezing up again. Issuing from the cabin, Stubb now called his boat’s crew, and pulled off for the stranger. Drawing across her bow, he perceived that in accordance with the fanciful French taste, the upper part of her stem-piece was carved in the likeness of a huge drooping stalk, was painted green, and for thorns had copper spikes projecting from it here and there; the whole terminating in a symmetrical folded bulb of a bright red colour. Upon her head boards, in large gilt letters, he read “Bouton de Rose,”—Rose-button, or Rose-bud; and this was the romantic name of this aromatic ship.
Though Stubb did not understand the Bouton part of the inscription, yet the word rose, and the bulbous figure-head put together, sufficiently explained the whole to him.
“A wooden rose-bud, eh?” he cried with his hand to his nose, “that will do very well; but how like all creation it smells!”
Now in order to hold direct communication with the people on deck, he had to pull round the bows to the starboard side, and thus come close to the blasted whale; and so talk over it.
Arrived then at this spot, with one hand still to his nose, he bawled—“Bouton-de-Rose, ahoy! are there any of you Bouton-de-Roses that speak English?”
“Yes,” rejoined a Guernsey-man from the bulwarks, who turned out to be the chief-mate.
“Well, then, my Bouton-de-Rose-bud, have you seen the White Whale?”
“What whale?”
“The White Whale—a Sperm Whale—Moby Dick, have ye seen him?
“Never heard of such a whale. Cachalot Blanche! White Whale—no.”
“Very good, then; good bye now, and I’ll call again in a minute.”

Then rapidly pulling back towards the Pequod, and seeing Ahab leaning over the quarter-deck rail awaiting his report, he moulded his two hands into a trumpet and shouted—“No, Sir! No!” Upon which Ahab retired, and Stubb returned to the Frenchman.
He now perceived that the Guernsey-man, who had just got into the chains, and was using a cutting-spade, had slung his nose in a sort of bag.
“What’s the matter with your nose, there?” said Stubb. “Broke it?”
“I wish it was broken, or that I didn’t have any nose at all!” answered the Guernsey-man, who did not seem to relish the job he was at very much. “But what are you holding yours for?”
“Oh, nothing! It’s a wax nose; I have to hold it on. Fine day, ain’t it? Air rather gardenny, I should say; throw us a bunch of posies, will ye, Bouton-de-Rose?”
“What in the devil’s name do you want here?” roared the Guernseyman, flying into a sudden passion.

“Oh! keep cool—cool? yes, that’s the word! why don’t you pack those whales in ice while you’re working at ’em? But joking aside, though; do you know, Rose-bud, that it’s all nonsense trying to get any oil out of such whales? As for that dried up one, there, he hasn’t a gill in his whole carcase.”

“I know that well enough; but, d’ye see, the Captain here won’t believe it; this is his first voyage; he was a Cologne manufacturer before. But come aboard, and mayhap he’ll believe you, if he won’t me; and so I’ll get out of this dirty scrape.”

“Anything to oblige ye, my sweet and pleasant fellow,” rejoined Stubb, and with that he soon mounted to the deck. There a queer scene presented itself. The sailors, in tasselled caps of red worsted, were getting the heavy tackles in readiness for the whales. But they worked rather slow and talked very fast, and seemed in anything but a good humor. All their noses upwardly projected from their faces like so many jib-booms. Now and then pairs of them would drop their work, and run up to the mast-head to get some fresh air. Some thinking they would catch the plague, dipped oakum in coal-tar, and at intervals held it to their nostrils. Others having broken the stems of their pipes almost short off at the bowl, were vigorously puffing tobacco-smoke, so that it constantly filled their olfactories.

Stubb was struck by a shower of outcries and anathemas proceeding from the Captain’s round-house abaft; and looking in that direction saw a fiery face thrust from behind the door, which was held ajar from within. This was the tormented surgeon, who, after in vain remonstrating against the proceedings of the day, had betaken himself to the Captain’s round-house (cabinet he called it) to avoid the pest; but still, could not help yelling out his entreaties and indignations at times.

Marking all this, Stubb argued well for his scheme, and turning to the Guernsey-man had a little chat with him, during which the stranger mate expressed his detestation of his Captain as a conceited ignoramus, who had brought them all into so unsavory and unprofitable a pickle. Sounding him carefully, Stubb further perceived that the Guernsey-man had not the slightest suspicion concerning the ambergris. He therefore held his peace on that head, but otherwise was quite frank and confidential with him, so that the two quickly concocted a little plan for both circumventing and satirizing the Captain, without his at all dreaming of distrusting their sincerity. According to this little plan of theirs, the Guernsey-man, under cover of an interpreter’s office, was to tell the Captain what he pleased, but as coming from Stubb; and as for Stubb, he was to utter any nonsense that should come uppermost in him during the interview.

By this time their destined victim appeared from his cabin. He was a small and dark, but rather delicate looking man for a sea-captain, with large whiskers and moustache, however; and wore a red cotton velvet vest with watch-seals at his side. To this gentleman, Stubb was now politely introduced by the Guernsey-man, who at once ostentatiously put on the aspect of interpreting between them.
“What shall I say to him first?” said he.
“Why,” said Stubb, eyeing the velvet vest and the watch and seals, “you may as well begin by telling him that he looks a sort of babyish to me, though I don’t pretend to be a judge.”

“He says, Monsieur,” said the Guernsey-man, in French, turning to his captain, “that only yesterday his ship spoke a vessel, whose captain and chief-mate, with six sailors, had all died of a fever caught from a blasted whale they had brought alongside.”
Upon this the captain started, and eagerly desired to know more.
“What now?” said the Guernsey-man to Stubb.

“Why, since he takes it so easy, tell him that now I have eyed him carefully, I’m quite certain that he’s no more fit to command a whale-ship than a St. Jago monkey. In fact, tell him from me he’s a baboon.”
“He vows and declares, Monsieur, that the other whale, the dried one, is far more deadly than the blasted one; in fine, Monsieur, he conjures us, as we value our lives, to cut loose from these fish.”
Instantly the captain ran forward, and in a loud voice commanded his crew to desist from hoisting the cutting-tackles, and at once cast loose the cables and chains confining the whales to the ship.
“What now?” said the Guernsey-man, when the Captain had returned to them.
“Why, let me see; yes, you may as well tell him now that—that—in fact, tell him I’ve diddled him, and (aside to himself) perhaps somebody else.”
“He says, Monsieur, that he’s very happy to have been of any service to us.”
Hearing this, the captain vowed that they were the grateful parties (meaning himself and mate) and concluded by inviting Stubb down into his cabin to drink a bottle of Bordeaux.
“He wants you to take a glass of wine with him,” said the interpreter.
“Thank him heartily; but tell him it’s against my principles to drink with the man I’ve diddled. In fact, tell him I must go.”

“He says, Monsieur, that his principles won’t admit of his drinking; but that if Monsieur wants to live another day to drink, then Monsieur had best drop all four boats, and pull the ship away from these whales, for it’s so calm they won’t drift.”

By this time Stubb was over the side, and getting into his boat, hailed the Guernsey-man to this effect,—that having a long tow-line in his boat, he would do what he could to help them, by pulling out the lighter whale of the two from the ship’s side. While the Frenchman’s boats, then, were engaged in towing the ship one way, Stubb benevolently towed away at his whale the other way, ostentatiously slacking out a most unusually long tow-line.

Presently a breeze sprang up; Stubb feigned to cast off from the whale; hoisting his boats, the Frenchman soon increased his distance, while the Pequod slid in between him and Stubb’s whale. Whereupon Stubb quickly pulled to the floating body, and hailing the Pequod to give notice of his intentions, at once proceeded to reap the fruit of his unrighteous cunning. Seizing his sharp boat-spade, he commenced an excavation in the body, a little behind the side fin. You would almost have thought he was digging a cellar there in the sea; and when at length his spade struck against the gaunt ribs, it was like turning up old Roman tiles and pottery buried in fat English loam. His boat’s crew were all in high excitement, eagerly helping their chief, and looking as anxious as gold-hunters.

And all the time numberless fowls were diving, and ducking, and screaming, and yelling, and fighting around them. Stubb was beginning to look disappointed, especially as the horrible nosegay increased, when suddenly from out the very heart of this plague, there stole a faint stream of perfume, which flowed through the tide of bad smells without being absorbed by it, as one river will flow into and then along with another, without at all blending with it for a time.
“I have it, I have it,” cried Stubb, with delight, striking something in the subterranean regions, “a purse! a purse!”

Dropping his spade, he thrust both hands in, and drew out handfuls of something that looked like ripe Windsor soap, or rich mottled old cheese; very unctuous and savory withal. You might easily dent it with your thumb; it is of a hue between yellow and ash colour. And this, good friends, is ambergris, worth a gold guinea an ounce to any druggist. Some six handfuls were obtained; but more was unavoidably lost in the sea, and still more, perhaps, might have been secured were it not for impatient Ahab’s loud command to Stubb to desist, and come on board, else the ship would bid them good bye.

Aye, and content too with scraping the dry bones of that other precious fish he has there. Poor devil! I say, pass round a hat, someone, and let's make him a present of a little oil for dear charity's sake. For what oil he'll get from that drugged whale there wouldn't be fit to burn in a jail — no, not in a condemned cell. And as for the other whale, why, I'll agree to get more oil by chopping up and boiling out these three masts of ours than he'll get from that bundle of bones. Though, now that I think of it, it may contain something worth a good deal more than oil. Yes — ambergris. I wonder now if our old man has thought of that. It's worth trying. Yes, I'm for it." And so saying he started for the quarter-deck.

By this time the faint breeze had become a complete calm, so that like it or not, the Pequod was now fairly trapped in the smell, with no hope of escaping unless the wind picked up again. Coming out of the cabin, Stubb called his boat's crew and pulled off for the stranger. Drawing across her bow, he saw that in accordance with the fanciful French taste, the upper part of her stem-piece was carved in the likeness of a huge drooping stalk, was painted green, and for thorns had copper spikes projecting from it here and there — the whole terminating in a symmetrical folded bulb of a bright red color. Upon her headboards, in large gilt letters, he read "Bouton de Rose" — Rose-button, or Rose-bud. And this was the romantic name of this aromatic ship.
Though Stubb did not understand the "Bouton" part of the inscription, the word "rose" and the bulbous figurehead put together sufficiently explained the whole to him.
"A wooden rose-bud, eh?" he cried with his hand to his nose. "That will do very well. But how like all creation it smells!"
Now in order to communicate directly with the people on deck, he had to pull around the bow to the starboard side, and thus come close to the blasted whale and talk over it.
Arriving at this spot, with one hand still to his nose, he bawled: "Bouton-de-Rose, ahoy! Are there any of you Bouton-de-Roses that speak English?"
"Yes," replied a Guernseyman from the bulwarks, who turned out to be the chief mate.
"Well then, my Bouton-de-Rose-bud, have you seen the White Whale?"
"What whale?"
"The White Whale — a Sperm Whale — Moby Dick. Have you seen him?"
"Never heard of such a whale. Cachalot Blanche! White Whale — no."
"Very good, then. Goodbye now, and I'll call again in a minute."

Then, pulling quickly back toward the Pequod and seeing Ahab leaning on the quarter-deck rail waiting for his report, he cupped his two hands into a trumpet and shouted, "No, sir! No!" At that, Ahab withdrew, and Stubb went back to the Frenchman.
He now saw that the Guernseyman, who had just climbed into the chains and was working with a cutting-spade, had his nose slung up in a kind of bag.
"What's the matter with your nose there?" said Stubb. "Broken it?"
"I wish it was broken, or that I didn't have any nose at all!" answered the Guernseyman, who did not seem to relish the job he was at very much. "But what are you holding yours for?"
"Oh, nothing! It's a wax nose — I have to hold it on. Fine day, isn't it? Air rather garden-like, I should say. Throw us a bunch of posies, will you, Bouton-de-Rose?"
"What in the devil's name do you want here?" roared the Guernseyman, flying into a sudden rage.

"Oh, keep cool — cool? Yes, that's the word! Why don't you pack those whales in ice while you're working at them? But joking aside, though — do you know, Rose-bud, that it's all nonsense trying to get any oil out of such whales? As for that dried-up one there, he hasn't a gill of oil in his whole carcass."

"I know that well enough. But, d'you see, the Captain here won't believe it. This is his first voyage — he was a Cologne manufacturer before. But come aboard, and maybe he'll believe you, if he won't believe me. And so I'll get out of this dirty mess."

"Anything to oblige you, my sweet and pleasant fellow," Stubb answered, and with that he was soon up on deck. A strange scene met him there. The sailors, in tasseled caps of red worsted, were getting the heavy tackles ready for the whales. But they worked rather slowly and talked very fast, and seemed in anything but a good mood. All their noses pointed upward from their faces like so many jib-booms. Every so often a couple of them would drop their work and run up to the masthead for some fresh air. Some, fearing they would catch the plague, dipped oakum in coal tar and held it to their nostrils from time to time. Others had snapped the stems of their pipes off almost at the bowl and were puffing hard on tobacco smoke, so that it kept their noses constantly full.

Stubb was struck by a shower of outcries and curses coming from the captain's round-house aft. Looking in that direction, he saw a fiery face thrust from behind the door, which was held slightly open from within. This was the tormented surgeon, who, after protesting in vain against the day's proceedings, had retreated to the captain's round-house ("cabinet," he called it) to avoid the pestilence — but still could not help yelling out his pleas and objections from time to time.

Noting all this, Stubb saw his opportunity. Turning to the Guernseyman, he had a little chat with him, during which the mate expressed his contempt for his captain as a conceited fool who had brought them all into so stinking and unprofitable a mess. Sounding him carefully, Stubb further perceived that the Guernseyman had not the slightest suspicion concerning the ambergris. He therefore kept quiet on that subject, but otherwise was quite frank and friendly with him, so that the two quickly hatched a little plan for both outwitting and mocking the captain, without his at all suspecting their true intentions. According to this plan, the Guernseyman, under cover of being an interpreter, was to tell the captain whatever he pleased, but as if it came from Stubb. And as for Stubb, he was to utter whatever nonsense came to mind during the interview.

By now their intended victim had come out of his cabin. He was a small, dark man, rather delicate-looking for a sea captain, though he did have large whiskers and a mustache; and he wore a red cotton-velvet vest with watch-seals at his side. The Guernseyman now introduced Stubb politely to this gentleman, and at once made a show of acting as interpreter between them.
"What shall I say to him first?" said he.
"Why," said Stubb, eyeing the velvet vest and the watch and seals, "you might as well start by telling him he looks kind of babyish to me, though I don't claim to be a judge."

"He says, Monsieur," said the Guernseyman in French, turning to his captain, "that only yesterday his ship spoke a vessel whose captain and chief mate, with six sailors, had all died of a fever caught from a blasted whale they had brought alongside."
Upon this the captain started, and eagerly wanted to know more.
"What now?" said the Guernseyman to Stubb.

"Why, since he takes it so easily, tell him that now I've eyed him carefully, I'm quite certain that he's no more fit to command a whale-ship than a St. Jago monkey. In fact, tell him from me he's a baboon."
"He vows and declares, Monsieur, that the other whale, the dried one, is far more deadly than the blasted one. In short, Monsieur, he begs us, as we value our lives, to cut loose from these fish."
At once the captain ran forward and shouted to his crew to stop hoisting the cutting-tackles and to cast off immediately the cables and chains that held the whales to the ship.
"What now?" said the Guernseyman, when the captain had returned to them.
"Why, let me see. Yes, you may as well tell him now that — that — in fact, tell him I've diddled him, and" — aside to himself — "perhaps somebody else."
"He says, Monsieur, that he's very happy to have been of any service to us."
Hearing this, the captain declared that they were the grateful parties — meaning himself and the mate — and concluded by inviting Stubb down to his cabin to drink a bottle of Bordeaux.
"He wants you to take a glass of wine with him," said the interpreter.
"Thank him heartily, but tell him it's against my principles to drink with the man I've diddled. In fact, tell him I must go."

"He says, Monsieur, that his principles won't allow him to drink. But that if Monsieur wants to live another day to drink, then Monsieur had best drop all four boats and pull the ship away from these whales, for it's so calm they won't drift."

By this time Stubb was over the side, and getting into his boat, he hailed the Guernseyman to this effect: that having a long tow-line in his boat, he would do what he could to help them by pulling out the lighter whale from the ship's side. While the Frenchman's boats were engaged in towing the ship one way, Stubb benevolently towed his whale the other way, ostentatiously letting out an unusually long tow-line.

Soon a breeze came up. Stubb made a show of casting off from the whale; the Frenchman hoisted his boats and quickly drew away, while the Pequod slipped in between him and Stubb's whale. At that, Stubb rowed swiftly to the floating body, hailed the Pequod to let them know what he meant to do, and at once set about reaping the fruit of his unrighteous cunning. Grabbing his sharp boat-spade, he began digging a hole in the body a little behind the side fin. You would almost have thought he was digging a cellar out there in the sea; and when his spade finally struck the gaunt ribs, it was like turning up old Roman tiles and pottery buried in fat English loam. His boat's crew were all wildly excited, eagerly helping their chief and looking as anxious as gold prospectors.

And all the while countless birds were diving and ducking and screaming and yelling and fighting around them. Stubb was starting to look disappointed, especially as the horrible nosegay grew stronger, when suddenly, from the very heart of this plague, a faint stream of perfume came stealing out. It ran through the tide of foul smells without being swallowed up by it, the way one river will flow into another and then run alongside it for a while without mixing at all.
"I have it! I have it!" cried Stubb with delight, striking something in the underground regions. "A purse! A purse!"

Dropping his spade, he plunged both hands in and pulled out handfuls of something that looked like ripe Windsor soap or rich, mottled old cheese, very oily and savory besides. You could easily dent it with your thumb; its color is somewhere between yellow and ash. And this, my good friends, is ambergris, worth a gold guinea an ounce to any druggist. About six handfuls were recovered; more was unavoidably lost in the sea, and still more might perhaps have been saved if impatient Ahab had not loudly ordered Stubb to stop and come aboard, or else the ship would say goodbye to them.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 91 — Pequod møder Rosenknoppen
paragraphs: »Det var forgæves at rode efter ambra i denne Leviatans bug, idet den uudholdelige stank forhindrede enhver undersøgelse.« — Sir T. Browne, V.E.

Det var en uge eller to efter den sidste hvalfangstscene, jeg har beskrevet. Vi sejlede langsomt over et søvnigt, diset middagshav, og her viste det sig, at de mange næser på Pequods dæk var skarpere udkig end de tre par øjne oppe i masten. Der kunne mærkes en mærkelig og ikke videre behagelig lugt over havet.
»Jeg vil vædde på noget,« sagde Stubb, »at der et sted i nærheden er nogle af de bedøvede hvaler, vi kildede forleden. Jeg tænkte nok, at de snart ville vende bugen i vejret.«

Lidt efter gled disen foran os til side, og der i det fjerne lå et skib, hvis beslåede sejl viste, at en eller anden slags hval måtte ligge langs siden. Da vi gled nærmere, viste den fremmede franske flag fra sin gaffel. Og af den hvirvlende sky af gribbelignende havfugle, der kredsede, svævede og styrtdykkede rundt om skibet, var det tydeligt, at hvalen langs siden måtte være det, fiskerne kalder en blasted whale — det vil sige en hval, der er død uforstyrret på havet og derfor er drevet rundt som et herreløst lig. Du kan nok forestille dig, hvilken ubehagelig lugt sådan en masse afgiver — værre end en assyrisk by under pesten, når de levende ikke kan nå at begrave de døde. Nogle finder den så uudholdelig, at ingen grådighed kan få dem til at fortøje ved siden af den. Alligevel er der nogle, der stadig gør det, uanset at olien fra sådanne dyr er af meget ringe kvalitet og på ingen måde minder om rosenolie.

Da vi på den døende vind kom endnu tættere på, så vi, at franskmanden havde endnu en hval liggende langs siden, og den virkede endnu mere som en blomsterbuket end den første. Den viste sig i virkeligheden at være en af de gådefulde hvaler, der ser ud til at skrumpe ind og dø af en vældig dyspepsi eller fordøjelsesbesvær, så deres døde kroppe er næsten helt blottet for noget, der ligner olie. Alligevel skal vi i rette tid se, at ingen kyndig fisker nogensinde vil rynke på næsen ad en hval som denne, hvor meget han end undgår fordærvede hvaler i almindelighed.
Pequod var nu kommet så tæt på den fremmede, at Stubb svor på, at han genkendte sin flensespadestang, viklet ind i linerne, der var knyttet rundt om halen på en af disse hvaler.

»Se nu den nette fyr,« lo han drillende og stod i skibets stævn. »Sikke en sjakal! Jeg ved godt, at de her franske Crappoer er ynkelige stakler til at fange hval. Nogle gange sætter de både i vandet for brænding, fordi de tror, det er kaskelothvaler, der blæser. Og nogle gange sejler de ud fra havn med lasten fuld af kasser med talglys og æsker med lyseslukkere, for de kan jo godt se, at al den olie, de får, ikke engang rækker til at dyppe kaptajnens væge i. Ja, det ved vi alle. Men se her, her er en Crappo, der er tilfreds med vores levninger — den bedøvede hval derovre, mener jeg. Ja, og tilfreds med at skrabe de tørre knogler af den anden dyrebare fisk, han har dér. Stakkels fyr! Hør, send en hat rundt, nogen, så vi kan give ham en lille smule olie som gave, ren og skær næstekærlighed. For den olie, han får af den bedøvede hval dér, ville ikke være god nok til at brænde i et fængsel — nej, ikke engang i en dødsdømts celle. Og hvad den anden hval angår, så vil jeg love at få mere olie ud af at hugge de tre master på vores skib i stykker og koge dem end af det bundt knogler. Men nu, hvor jeg tænker på det, kan det måske indeholde noget, der er meget mere værd end olie. Ja — ambra. Mon vores gamle har tænkt på det? Det er værd at prøve. Ja, jeg er med.« Og med de ord gik han mod agterdækket.

På dette tidspunkt var den svage brise blevet til vindstille, så Pequod, om den ville eller ej, nu sad ordentligt fanget i stanken uden håb om at slippe væk, medmindre vinden tog til igen. Stubb kom ud af kahytten, kaldte sin båds besætning sammen og roede over til den fremmede. Da han kom på tværs af hendes bov, så han, at den øverste del af forstavnen var udskåret i et fantasifuldt fransk mønster som en kæmpemæssig, nedhængende stilk, malet grøn, med kobbertorne, der stak ud her og der, og det hele endte i et symmetrisk, sammenfoldet løg i skarp rød farve. På hendes stævnbrædder læste han med store forgyldte bogstaver »Bouton de Rose« — Rosenknop, eller Rose-bud. Og det var det romantiske navn på dette vellugtende skib.
Stubb forstod ikke »Bouton« i indskriften, men ordet »rose« og den løgformede galionsfigur forklarede tilsammen det hele rigeligt for ham.
»En rosenknop af træ, hva'?« råbte han med hånden for næsen. »Det er fint nok. Men hvor den dog stinker, så det forslår!«
For at kunne tale direkte med folkene på dækket måtte han nu ro rundt om stævnen til styrbord side og dermed komme tæt på den fordærvede hval og tale hen over den.
Da han nåede dertil, stadig med den ene hånd for næsen, brølede han: »Bouton-de-Rose, ohøj! Er der nogen af jer Bouton-de-Roser, der taler engelsk?«
»Ja,« svarede en mand fra Guernsey oppe fra essingen, og det viste sig at være førstestyrmanden.
»Nå, så, min Bouton-de-Rose-knop, har du set den hvide hval?«
»Hvad for en hval?«
»Den hvide hval — en kaskelot — Moby Dick. Har du set ham?«
»Har aldrig hørt om sådan en hval. Cachalot Blanche! Hvid hval — nej.«
»Godt så. Farvel for nu, jeg kommer tilbage om et øjeblik.«

Så roede han hurtigt tilbage mod Pequod, og da han så Ahab læne sig mod rælingen på agterdækket og vente på hans melding, satte han begge hænder for munden som en tragt og råbte: »Nej, sir! Nej!« Derpå trak Ahab sig tilbage, og Stubb roede tilbage til franskmanden.
Nu så han, at manden fra Guernsey, som lige var klatret op i rusten og var i gang med en flensespade, havde fået næsen bundet op i en slags pose.
»Hvad er der i vejen med din næse?« sagde Stubb. »Har du brækket den?«
»Gid den var brækket, eller gid jeg slet ikke havde nogen næse!« svarede manden fra Guernsey, som ikke så ud til at nyde sit arbejde ret meget. »Men hvorfor holder du på din?«
»Åh, ingenting! Det er en voksnæse — jeg må holde den på. Dejlig dag, ikke? Luften er næsten som i en have, vil jeg sige. Kast os en buket blomster, vil du, Bouton-de-Rose?«
»Hvad fanden vil du her?« brølede manden fra Guernsey og blev pludselig rasende.

»Åh, tag det roligt — køligt? Ja, det er det rette ord! Hvorfor pakker du ikke de hvaler i is, mens du arbejder på dem? Men spøg til side — ved du hvad, Rosenknop, det er noget sludder at prøve at få olie ud af den slags hvaler. Og den udtørrede dér har ikke en pægl olie i hele sit kadaver.«

»Det ved jeg godt. Men ser du, kaptajnen her vil ikke tro det. Det er hans første rejse — han var fabrikant fra Cologne før. Men kom om bord, så tror han dig måske, hvis han ikke vil tro mig. Så kommer jeg væk fra dette ækle rod.«

»Alt for at gøre dig en tjeneste, min søde og rare ven,« svarede Stubb, og med de ord var han snart oppe på dækket. Et mærkeligt syn mødte ham. Sømændene, med kvastede huer af rødt kamgarn, var i gang med at gøre de tunge taljer klar til hvalerne. Men de arbejdede ret langsomt og snakkede meget hurtigt, og de så alt andet end veloplagte ud. Alle deres næser pegede opad fra ansigterne som så mange klyverbomme. Med mellemrum slap et par af dem arbejdet og løb op i masten efter frisk luft. Nogle, der frygtede at få pesten, dyppede værk i stenkulstjære og holdt det op for næseborene en gang imellem. Andre havde knækket piberørene af næsten helt nede ved piben og pustede hårdt tobaksrøg, så deres næser hele tiden var fulde af den.

Et skred af skrig og forbandelser fra kaptajnens runde agterhus ramte Stubb. Da han så derhen, fik han øje på et ildrødt ansigt, der blev stukket frem bag døren, som blev holdt på klem indefra. Det var den plagede skibslæge, som efter forgæves at have protesteret mod dagens fremgangsmåde havde trukket sig tilbage til kaptajnens runde agterhus (»kabinettet,« kaldte han det) for at undgå smitten — men som stadig ikke kunne lade være med at råbe sine bønner og indvendinger ud en gang imellem.

Da Stubb så alt dette, fik han sin chance. Han vendte sig til manden fra Guernsey og snakkede lidt med ham, og under samtalen lod styrmanden sin foragt for sin kaptajn komme til udtryk: en indbildsk tåbe, som havde bragt dem alle ud i så stinkende og ulønsomt et rod. Efter forsigtigt at have sonderet ham kunne Stubb yderligere mærke, at manden fra Guernsey ikke havde den mindste mistanke om ambraen. Han tav derfor om det, men var ellers helt åben og venlig over for ham, så de to hurtigt udklækkede en lille plan om både at narre og gøre grin med kaptajnen, uden at han overhovedet anede deres sande hensigter. Ifølge planen skulle manden fra Guernsey, under dække af at være tolk, fortælle kaptajnen, hvad han lystede, men som om det kom fra Stubb. Og Stubb skulle for sin del sige, hvad der end faldt ham ind af vrøvl under samtalen.

Nu var deres påtænkte offer kommet ud fra sin kahyt. Han var en lille, mørk mand, ret spinkel at se til for en søkaptajn, selv om han havde store bakkenbarter og overskæg, og han bar en rød vest af bomuldsfløjl med urgehæng ved siden. Manden fra Guernsey præsenterede nu høfligt Stubb for denne herre og gik straks i gang med at spille tolk mellem dem.
»Hvad skal jeg sige til ham først?« sagde han.

»Jo,« sagde Stubb og betragtede fløjlsvesten og uret og gehænget, »du kan lige så godt begynde med at fortælle ham, at han ser lidt barnagtig ud i mine øjne, selv om jeg ikke giver mig ud for at være dommer.«

»Han siger, monsieur,« sagde manden fra Guernsey på fransk og vendte sig mod sin kaptajn, »at hans skib først i går mødte et fartøj, hvis kaptajn og førstestyrmand sammen med seks matroser alle var døde af en feber, de havde fået fra en fordærvet hval, som de havde taget ind langs skibssiden.«
Ved det fór kaptajnen sammen og ville ivrigt vide mere.
»Hvad nu?« sagde manden fra Guernsey til Stubb.

»Jo, siden han tager det så roligt, så fortæl ham, at nu hvor jeg har set nøje på ham, er jeg ganske sikker på, at han er lige så egnet til at føre et hvalfangerskib som en abe fra St. Jago. Ja, sig ham fra mig, at han er en bavian.«

»Han sværger og forsikrer, monsieur, at den anden hval, den udtørrede, er langt farligere end den fordærvede. Kort sagt, monsieur, han beder os, hvis vi sætter pris på vores liv, om at skære os løs fra disse fisk.«
Straks løb kaptajnen frem og råbte til sit mandskab, at de skulle holde op med at hejse skæretaljerne og med det samme kaste de tove og kæder af, der holdt hvalerne fast til skibet.
»Hvad nu?« sagde manden fra Guernsey, da kaptajnen var kommet tilbage til dem.
»Jo, lad mig se. Ja, du kan lige så godt sige til ham nu, at — at — ja, sig ham, at jeg har narret ham, og« — hen for sig selv — »måske en anden også.«
»Han siger, monsieur, at han er meget glad for at have kunnet være os til tjeneste.«
Da kaptajnen hørte det, erklærede han, at det var dem, der skyldte tak — han mente sig selv og styrmanden — og afsluttede med at invitere Stubb ned i sin kahyt for at drikke en flaske bordeaux.
»Han vil have, at du tager et glas vin sammen med ham,« sagde tolken.
»Tak ham hjerteligt, men sig, at det er imod mine principper at drikke sammen med den mand, jeg har narret. Sig ham i øvrigt, at jeg må af sted.«

»Han siger, monsieur, at hans principper ikke tillader ham at drikke. Men at hvis monsieur ønsker at leve en dag til for at drikke, så er det bedst, at monsieur sætter alle fire både i vandet og får skibet slæbt væk fra disse hvaler, for det er så vindstille, at de ikke vil drive væk.«

På dette tidspunkt var Stubb over rælingen, og da han kom ned i sin båd, anråbte han manden fra Guernsey og fortalte ham, at da han havde en lang slæbeline i båden, ville han gøre, hvad han kunne for at hjælpe dem ved at trække den lettere hval væk fra skibssiden. Mens franskmandens både var i gang med at slæbe skibet den ene vej, slæbte Stubb velvilligt sin hval den anden vej og firede demonstrativt en usædvanlig lang slæbeline ud.

Snart kom der en brise. Stubb lod, som om han kastede hvalen af, franskmanden hejste sine både og trak hurtigt væk, mens Pequod gled ind mellem ham og Stubbs hval. Ved det roede Stubb hurtigt ud til det flydende legeme, anråbte Pequod for at lade dem vide, hvad han havde i sinde, og gik straks i gang med at høste frugten af sin uretfærdige snedighed. Han greb sin skarpe bådspade og begyndte at grave et hul i kroppen lidt bag sidefinnen. Man skulle næsten have troet, at han gravede en kælder derude i havet, og da hans spade til sidst ramte de magre ribben, var det, som om man vendte gamle romerske tegl og lerkar op, nedgravet i fed engelsk lerjord. Hele hans bådsbesætning var vildt ophidset, hjalp ivrigt deres chef og så lige så spændt ud som guldgravere.

Og hele tiden dykkede, dukkede, skreg, hylede og sloges utallige fugle rundt om dem. Stubb var begyndt at se skuffet ud, især fordi den rædselsfulde buket blev stærkere, da der pludselig midt fra pestens hjerte kom en svag strøm af duft sivende. Den løb gennem strømmen af modbydelige lugte uden at blive opslugt af den, ligesom en flod kan løbe ud i en anden og så et stykke tid løbe side om side uden overhovedet at blande sig.
»Jeg har den! Jeg har den!« råbte Stubb henrykt, da han ramte noget i de underjordiske egne. »En pung! En pung!«

Han tabte spaden, stak begge hænder ned og trak håndfulde op af noget, der lignede moden Windsor-sæbe eller fed, spættet gammel ost, og som desuden var meget olieagtigt og vellugtende. Man kunne let trykke et mærke i det med tommelfingeren, og farven ligger et sted mellem gul og askegrå. Og dette, mine gode venner, er ambra, som en apoteker gerne betaler en gylden guinea for pr. ounce. Der blev reddet omkring seks håndfulde; mere gik uundgåeligt tabt i havet, og endnu mere kunne måske være reddet, hvis den utålmodige Ahab ikke højlydt havde beordret Stubb til at holde op og komme om bord, ellers ville skibet sige farvel til dem.
